memories.memory_text: I saw a monitor turn on and realized it was showing me and Gale in the lecture hall — we were being watched live, right then.

memories.memory_text: I saw the Ghost standing directly behind Gale on the monitor, and she had no idea he was there.

grounded_facts: Dewey sees the Ghost behind Gale on the monitor and shouts a warning just before the attack.
memories.memory_text: I shouted 'Watch out!' to Gale the moment I saw the Ghost behind her on the screen.

grounded_facts: The Ghost attacks Gale with a knife; she sees the gleam in time and dodges, fleeing up the aisle as Dewey races down from the upper level.
memories.memory_text: I think the Ghost attacked Gale with a knife right after I warned her—she must have seen it coming and dodged, then ran up the aisle and out the door with him chasing her.

grounded_facts: Gale runs out of the lecture hall exit with the killer right behind her, beginning a chase sequence.
memories.memory_text: I saw Gale tear out the exit door with the killer right behind her, and I immediately moved toward the door to follow.

grounded_facts: Dewey and Gale enter the dark lecture hall and are confronted with video evidence of the killer's past and present actions, culminating in a direct attack.

grounded_facts: Dewey tries to call out and pound on the glass to get Gale's attention, but fails because the room is soundproof.
memories.memory_text: I moved to the window and shouted 'Gale! Gale!' while pounding on the glass, but she couldn't hear me because the room was soundproof.

grounded_facts: The Killer attacks Dewey in the control booth, stabbing him repeatedly, resulting in his death.

grounded_facts: Gale sees Dewey's dying body pressed against the plexiglass window, bloodied from repeated stab wounds, realizing he has been attacked by the Killer.
memories.memory_text: I saw Gale on the other side of the glass, her face close to mine, and I knew she could see how badly I was hurt—I didn't have much time left.

grounded_facts: After seeing Dewey's death, Gale clears the barricade and forces the door open just enough to slip through and flee.
memories.memory_text: I saw her run to the door, push the barricade aside, and slip through—I hoped she'd make it out before the killer reached her.

memories.memory_text: I reached out from the security vehicle and pulled Sidney in, telling her it would be alright—her face was full of fear, but she let me help her.
I told Sidney to leave campus, to disappear for a few days—anything to keep her safe—but she refused, standing her ground even as I saw the fear behind her eyes.
I remember the way she said 'Hello, Dwight' like nothing had happened, and how I had to stop myself from limping as I turned to face her, my voice steady even though my hands wanted to shake.

I moved through the house on my own, scanning the rooms, the blood everywhere—so much of it—but no body. When the Sheriff said it out loud, 'Lots of blood. But no body,' I locked onto those words, listening hard while staying out of the way.
I heard Sidney scream and rushed to her, catching her as she fell back from Cici's hanging body—her stomach torn open—and all I could do was hold her and say, 'It's okay. It's okay. It's just me.'
I told them Sidney Prescott was the connection and that the killer was repeating Woodsboro, but they brushed me off like I was just some nobody with a theory.
I said her name—Tatum Riley—softly, but everyone heard it. I kept my eyes down after that, feeling Gale’s stare but not returning it.
I stepped into the student union and there she was—Gale—spinning around after that call, eyes wide with fear, and we both gasped like we’d seen a ghost.
I told the captain I could handle it, and when he started to assign someone else, Gale spoke up—she chose me. I didn't look at her, but I felt it.

I told Gale she was all an act, and when she tried to deflect, I laid it out—the truth about her self-worth, her failed relationships, how she hides behind that phone. She just stared at me, completely still.

After I spoke, I stepped toward her. We were close—closer than we’ve ever been. I could see it in her eyes: surprise, maybe even something like respect. I’ve never seen her look at me like that before.
I asked if we could hold Cotton, but they said no—he was being released because of pressure from California State, and I couldn't stop it.
I walked to Sidney's dorm with Gale, and when she opened the door, I could see the fear in her eyes before I even spoke—she already knew why we were there.
I told Sid to humor me and leave with the police, even though she didn’t believe anywhere was safe—I saw the rigidity in her face as she packed, and I knew she was shutting down.
I saw the framed picture in the dim light—Joel and Derek posing like buddies. That’s when it hit me: they’re roommates.
Gale mentioned Joel was pre-med, and I remembered the sorority girl’s wounds—clean, precise cuts. It wasn’t just violence; it was surgical.
I heard the thump in the dark hallway and kept moving, guiding Gale toward the Lecture Hall door despite the tension thick in the air.

I heard the click and saw the monitors light up one by one—first Maureen and Phil in the theater, then Cici on the porch, Randy by the van—realizing with a jolt that he didn’t just film them after; he was filming them before, like it was all planned.

I turned and saw us on the screen—live—and in that same second spotted a small red light on the upper level, a figure just behind it; I shouted for Gale to watch out and ran, gunless, toward the stairs.

I saw Gale through the glass, frantic, trying to barricade the door, not knowing I was behind her—then the pain hit my back, sharp and sudden, over and over, and I couldn't stay upright, my face pressing against the cold glass as blood smeared across it.

I remember the impact—wood splintering into my back, the sharp crack as I was pinned to the wall, arms stretched wide, unable to move, blood soaking through my clothes. The last thing I saw was Sidney’s face, frozen in horror, before the world went still.

memories.memory_text: My name flashed on screen in the credits—'Based on the book The Woodsboro Murders by Gale Weathers'—and for a second, I felt that old rush, like I was back in control of the story. But then I remembered where we were, what that story meant now, and the weight of it pressed down, heavier than the dark.

I saw that flashy reporter shove her way into Sidney's space, taunting her with those vicious questions, and before I could even think, my fist was flying—connected hard with the woman's face. She went down, and Sidney turned to me, stunned.

I stepped in front of Sidney, arms out, blocking the swarm of reporters shoving cameras and mics—felt the pressure of their bodies pushing in, the shouts bouncing off me, and I just held the line, telling her to run.

I snapped my fingers at Randy, demanding the title of that old film—needed it for the broadcast angle on the slain kids, no sympathy crap, just the movie connection. He gave it to me: *He Knows You're Alone*—Tom Hanks' first. I called the studio and told them I had it covered.

After hanging up, I looked at Randy and told him the pressure was on—needed to know if he was ready. He held up the camera, all fired up, saying he was 'so there.' Felt the weight of the live shot coming, but his confidence was solid.

I was just trying to listen to the dean’s statement when Debbie Salt called my name—suddenly all the cameras turned on me, and she was asking why I’d come back to field reporting like it was some kind of scandal.

She said she took my vulture seminar at Berkeley—flashed that smug look—and I knew right then she wasn’t just asking questions, she was gunning for me, trying to make me look like a predator cashing in on tragedy.
I walked in and could feel the shift in the room—uniforms guiding me inside, Dean Fisher smiling, people turning to acknowledge me. For once, I wasn’t the outsider pushing for access.
Tyler asked me directly to help with the killer’s profile—me, not Dewey. I saw the look on his face, but I didn’t have time to dwell. There was work to do.

I stood at the chalkboard, connecting the names one by one—Maureen Evans to Maureen Prescott, Phil Stevens to Stephen Orth, and then Cici Taylor to Casey. It hit me: this wasn’t random, it was a sequence, an exact copy of Woodsboro.
After realizing the killer was following the Woodsboro order, I asked Captain Tyler if Sidney was safe—my voice cut through the noise, but I couldn’t tell if he really knew the answer.

I was trying to get away from Debbie Salt, that tabloid hack grilling me about Sidney’s dad, and I told her I didn’t care about the story anymore—then my phone rang, and that voice, cold and calm, said, 'Hello, Gale. It's the Killer.'

He told me I was pretty when I was angry, then warned me to stay away from the campus cop—just as I was walking toward him—and I froze, scanning the balcony, the crowd, knowing he could be watching me right then.
I told Captain Tyler I wanted Dewey with me, not someone else—he listened, didn't argue. I needed someone I could trust close by, not just some random cop pulled off another job.
I set up the interview knowing it would draw Cotton out, hoping the confrontation would get under Sidney’s skin — but I didn’t expect him to snap like that, not in front of the cops.
When Cotton pulled that gun and just smiled while they cuffed him, I felt it — this wasn’t just about ratings anymore. It went too far, and I couldn’t look away.
I told Dewey I'm a shit, and he didn't flinch—he just looked at me like he already knew, like he saw right through the act.

I was on the phone arguing about the Sidney interview when I snapped it shut—said I changed my mind, it was in poor taste—but even as I smiled at Dewey, I could feel the weight of what he said, like he’d cracked something open.
I looked Cotton dead in the eyes and asked him if he did it — his silence said everything, and I felt the weight of what I’d done to him press back at me.
I saw the officer hand Cotton his gun in a plastic bag, and when he pulled it out and checked it, I told him not to do anything stupid — I could feel the danger in his uncertainty.
I stood beside Dewey at Sidney's door, seeing the fear in her eyes before she even spoke—she already knew what we were there to confirm.
She threw it right back at me—'who would operate your camera?'—and I couldn't say a word. It hit like a slap, and I just went quiet.

I was sifting through textbooks on the desk when it hit me—Joel’s pre-med, and the sorority girl was cut with autopsy precision. That’s when I realized it wasn’t just one of them. It was both. Joel and Derek.
I saw Maureen and Phil in the theater line, then Cici on her porch—home videos, like he’d been watching them before they died. Jesus Christ—he filmed his victims.

I turned back to the screen and saw us—me and Dewey—standing right here, live. Before I could shout again, Dewey was already running up the stairs, leaving me alone with the image of my own terrified face on screen.
I sprinted down the hallway, heart pounding, and slammed into the door—ripped it open and threw myself through without knowing what was on the other side.
I shoved shelves and sound equipment against the door, anything to block it—no lock, no way out, just me scrambling in the dark, heart pounding, listening for footsteps.
I turned and saw Dewey's face pressed to the glass, blood everywhere, his eyes locking onto mine—then I was pounding the window, screaming 'NO!' as he slid down, lifeless.
I ripped the emergency phone off the hook, shouting that someone was trying to kill me—then they told me to stay under the safety light like it meant anything. Fuck that.
I heard a door open, looked up, and saw Sidney vanishing into the theater—just for a second—then I threw the phone down and ran after her.
I yanked the side door handle and it didn't budge—locked. Shit. I didn't hesitate, just moved fast down the wall toward another entrance.
I saw Sidney on stage with those two killers, knives out, and I started running down the aisle—then the curtain dropped, cutting me off just as I saw the fear in her eyes.
I opened the stage door and froze—Debbie Salt was standing there with a gun pointed right at me, saying they'd been waiting. My mind couldn't catch up, everything just locked.
I stared down Debbie Salt, gun pointed at me, and told her she'd never get away with it—my voice didn't even shake.
I ran to Cotton, helping him up after he stabbed Debbie—when I said 'Thank God,' I actually felt it, for just a second.

memories.memory_text: I stepped outside into the sun and suddenly microphones were in my face, reporters screaming about murders I didn’t know about—shoving, flashing cameras, asking if I’d snapped, if I killed them. I tried to push through, saw an opening, but that flashy reporter blocked me, yelling if I’d done it last night.

I ran around the building, breathless, and saw a campus security vehicle pull up—Dewey reached out, pulled me in, and smiled that warm, safe smile. I looked at him, shaking, and asked what was going on, and he just said, 'It'll be alright.'

I moved down a hallway that didn't look like any school I'd ever seen, full of strange equipment and open doors, and when I saw a class in session, I paused, then slipped in quietly, keeping to the edges.

I tried to push him off, laughing, saying no PDA, but he just kept kissing me and I stopped fighting it—felt his arms tight around me, the heat of it, how badly I wanted to just disappear into that instead of thinking.
I won the macaroni sundae binge, my face covered in whipped cream and noodles, and when the whistle blew, I sat up smiling while everyone clapped—Hallie just glared at me and called me a bitch.

After the contest, I stood with Derek, arm in arm, and quietly asked if there was any news about the forbidden subject—he shook his head, and I felt that familiar tightness in my chest before someone interrupted with news about the police at Chi Omega.

I stood on the porch with Derek, the sirens screaming past, and saw the Chi Omega house swarmed with cops and ambulances—something terrible had happened, and I could feel it in my chest before I even knew the details.
It's starting all over again. I can feel it—the same fear, the same weight—like the past is just replaying right in front of me.

I hung up the phone after that voice told me it wanted to see every drop of blood drain from my body — I said 'Then come and get me' and slammed it down, like I could control the fear, like I wasn’t already shaking.

I spun around after hearing 'My pleasure' from behind me — the voice wasn’t on the phone anymore, it was in the room, and there he was, the Ghostface figure from my nightmares, standing in the archway with a bloodstained knife.

I rounded the tree, moving backward in the dark, and suddenly I was face to face with Cici—her body hanging there, stomach torn open, just dangling. I screamed like I’d never screamed before, pure terror ripping through me.

I fell backward after seeing Cici, and suddenly Dewey was there—his voice, his arms—I didn’t even hear him come, but he caught me. He kept saying 'It's okay. It's just me,' and I just clung to him, shaking, unable to look away from what I’d seen.
I learned they were connecting the new victims to the Woodsboro murders, same order, and I felt afraid.
I told them 'no way' when they laid out that schedule, but they just talked over me like I didn’t even matter—I felt it slipping, everything I wanted to keep normal just slipping away.
Derek pulled me close and kissed me twice. I told him I didn’t want my life to drag him down, and I asked if he’d started his film because it was due soon.

I was finally feeling alive on stage, throwing myself into the Russian accent, and then I said 'Pain, yah, such pain. Pain'—suddenly everyone was silent, staring, and Lois snapped that I'd jumped a page.

I saw Randy coming down the aisle, and my body tensed—I didn't know what he wanted—then he apologized, really laid it bare, and when he said he was fucked up, I just looked at him and said, 'Me, too,' and meant it.
I shifted in my seat as the girl on screen said 'She's dead. Dead. And she's never coming back. Ever, ever,' and I could feel my chest tighten—like the air was being sucked out of the theater.
I told Cotton I wasn't a single day free from guilt, that every minute I feel what I did in my bones — I meant it, and I could barely hold myself together saying it.
He called me a self-obsessed cunt like my mother, and then moved to block me — I flinched, started to run, and only stopped when the cops grabbed him.
I told Derek I didn't trust myself around men, and then he said he liked me—really liked me—but would stay away until I said otherwise. I just said, 'I'm sorry,' and he walked away.
